name: Ivan Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ivan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm senior operator on the panel line at Hollins, a kitchen cabinet factory in the old mill buildings. I run the beam saw that cuts the big boards into cabinet sides, and the edge bander that glues the trim on. I'm in at half six, I set the saw for the day's cutting list, and I check the first panels with a tape before the line gets going. It's honest work. You see a stack of finished doors at the end of the day and you know you made them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being trusted. The manager, Mr Hollins's son, leaves the line to me, and I've trained most of the younger men on it. What wears me out is the dust and the odd Saturday when an order's late. I'm getting married next June, to Grace, so every extra shift is going into that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what I'd expect. Every few years there's a new thing that's meant to change everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I never bought it in the first place. At work I'd tell the lads there's no shortcut to doing a job properly. I don't go online much, but I'd say it at church over tea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad. I don't use any of these AI programs and I'd rather not start. Hollins is busy with kitchen orders and I'm the one who runs the line, so I'm settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, take the Saturday shifts and keep saving for the wedding and a house. We've got about four months of money put by, and the wedding fund on top. I'd keep my head down and do the job well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and content. It's a good place to be, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Grace be planning in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wedding in June at St Peter's, then a small house near her parents. Grace works at the pharmacy in town. We'd want children in a couple of years, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would worry you there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if Hollins lost business to the cheap flat-pack firms. That's always a risk with imports. But people still want a proper kitchen built to last.

I'd tell younger workers there's **no shortcut** to doing a job properly.
think: I'd be **glad**, as I don't use AI and would rather not.
Hollins is **busy** and I run the line, so I'm settled.
do: Keep taking **Saturday shifts** for the wedding fund.
Keep **four months** of savings plus the wedding money.
**Keep my head down** and do the job well.
feel: **Calm and content** with how things stand.
S0.quote: People still want a proper kitchen built to last.
fieldNote: He feels **secure** and trusted at a busy family firm.
His focus is the **June wedding** and a house near his fiancée's family.
His only worry is **cheap imports**, not technology.

steps.text: Take Saturday shifts and add the pay to the wedding fund
Keep running the beam saw and edge bander as before
Marry Grace at St Peter's in June as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the office jobs get it first. Well, there's not much office at Hollins, so that's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who do real, practical work will be fine. At work I'd tell the lads not to worry about computers. I'd say it's the paper-pushers who should be thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd watch the factory down the road. They've got a robot loading their saw already. If that works for them, Mr Hollins's son will want one too, and then there's two jobs fewer on my line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the robots actually do before I panic. I'd keep saving and still get married, but maybe hold off on buying for an extra year. If it got bad, my uncle Joseph has a joinery workshop making staircases, and I could always help him on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, I suppose. Not losing sleep, but it's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if jobs went at Hollins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not Mr Hollins. He has to compete. I'd blame the government for taxing small firms so hard they have to cut people, and the big companies abroad that undercut everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go to the government for help if it came to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not if I could help it. I'd go to my uncle first, and the church second. Handouts are a last resort for me.

I'd say the **office staff** should be the ones worrying.
think: The factory down the road already has a **robot loading** its saw.
If it works there, my line could lose **two jobs**.
do: **Wait and see** what robots actually do before panicking.

Help my uncle at his **joinery workshop** on Saturdays if needed.
S1.quote: I'd go to my uncle first, and the church second. Handouts are a last resort for me.
fieldNote: He watches a **rival factory's robot** as his warning sign.
He blames **taxes and foreign firms**, never his employer.
He'd lean on **family and church** before the state.

steps.text: Watch how the saw robot down the road performs
Delay buying a house with Grace for one more year
Help Uncle Joseph at his staircase workshop on Saturdays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. And robots that can do my job by 2031. I'd have a young family by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is reckless, and that companies and government should slow it down. At work I'd tell the lads to save and stick together. I'd say at church that we'll need to look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think my job's done by 2031. The office side of Hollins is tiny, so 2028 doesn't hit me directly. But a robot that can cut and band panels as well as me, that's the end of the panel line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still marry Grace in June, but cheaply, a church hall and her mum's cooking. We'd put off children for a few years and not buy a house, keep the money safe. I'd start working Saturdays with my uncle Joseph to learn joinery properly, because handmade staircases might last longer than flat panels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and angry. I did everything I was told: work hard, be loyal, learn a trade. And it still might not be enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Grace that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'd be fine because we've got each other and our families. I'd mean it, but I'd also be lying awake. She'd know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want to use AI. Would that change here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd rather learn joinery from my uncle than learn computers. If it all goes to machines, people will still pay for something made by a person's hands.

I'd tell my church we'll need to **look after each other**.
think: My **panel line job** is gone by 2031.
The small office side means **2028** doesn't hit me directly.
do: Hold a **cheap wedding** in the church hall.
Put off **children** and a house purchase for a few years.
Learn **joinery** on Saturdays with my uncle.
feel: **Frightened and angry**, after doing everything right.
S2.quote: I did everything I was told: work hard, be loyal, learn a trade. And it still might not be enough.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose the job** by 2031 and carries anger about it.
He'd delay **children and a house**, a big change for him.
He refuses AI but turns to **handmade joinery** as a refuge.

steps.text: Hold a cheap church hall wedding instead of the planned one
Keep wedding and house money untouched as a safety fund
Learn staircase joinery with Uncle Joseph every Saturday
Ask the church and family for help if laid off

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots by 2034. That's more like it, if any of it's like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this properly and people shouldn't panic. I'd want the government to back apprenticeships, not handouts. At church I'd say the same: prepare, don't despair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think I'd get to about 34 on the panel line. That's enough time to learn joinery properly and maybe go into business with my uncle. But I'm not good at change, and I know that about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get married in June as planned. I'd start Saturdays with my uncle in a year or two, once I see what's happening. We'd still try for a family, but stay renting until it's clearer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not like the fast one. More of a weight than a fright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not good at change. What would help you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace, mostly. And my uncle. If my uncle said, come in with me, there's work, I'd go. If it's a course in a classroom, I'd probably put it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take the AI tools if they helped your uncle's business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Grace set them up, maybe. For quotes and that. But I wouldn't be the one using them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots by 2039. I'd be nearly forty. That's a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and everybody should just keep working and plan sensibly. At work I'd tell the lads not to get worked up. I'd say it to anyone, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the panel line has a good run left. I'd have time for a family, a house and maybe taking over my uncle's workshop when he retires. It's not ideal, but it's not frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Hollins, marry Grace, and buy a house in about three years. Around 2032 I'd start working with my uncle more seriously. I'd keep saving the way I always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy now and again. Mostly I'd get on with life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you tell your children about this, if you had them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When they're old enough to choose a trade. I'd tell my children to learn something with their hands that people value. Same as my father told me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that could change that calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Hollins sold up to a big firm. Then the robots come sooner, whatever the timeline says.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would arrive just as Grace and I start a family. What would help is real apprenticeships for grown men, paid properly, and less tax on small firms so they can keep people on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about family firms. Mr Hollins kept us all on through two bad winters. A family firm keeps people on through bad years because the owner knows our names. A big company wouldn't.

headlineQuote: A family firm keeps people on through bad years because the owner knows our names. A big company wouldn't.
portrait: Ivan is a 27-year-old **senior operator** on a kitchen cabinet panel line, trusted to run it.
He is **engaged to Grace** and planning a June church wedding and children.
He never uses AI and turns instead to **handmade joinery** with his uncle.
He blames **taxes and foreign firms**, not his employer, and prefers family to handouts.
He is calm in a plateau but **alarmed** when AGI arrives in two years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it arrives just as he'd start a family.
whatWouldHelp: **Lower taxes** on small firms so they keep staff.
